contributions: An openly licensed (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0) comprehensive real analysis textbook with 761 numbered exercises and 295 worked examples; judged to meet evaluation criteria of the American Institute of Mathematics Open Textbook Initiative
limitations: The book explicitly notes it does not develop the real numbers from their axioms but assumes familiarity with consequences except completeness. It acknowledges that the transition from elementary calculus to rigorous analysis is increasingly difficult for today's students. Chapter 3.5 on Lebesgue's criterion can be omitted without compromising subsequent material. The instructor's solution manual is not freely available (reserved by the author).
methods: The book systematically develops real analysis from the axiomatic foundations of the real number system (field properties, order, completeness) through one-variable differential and integral calculus, infinite sequences and series, multivariable real-valued and vector-valued functions, multiple integrals, and finally metric spaces. Chapters 1–5 cover real-valued functions and require only elementary calculus; Chapters 6–7 require linear algebra; Chapter 8 follows from Chapters 1–5.
results: The text presents the real numbers as a complete ordered field with axioms (A)–(I), proving key results including the Triangle Inequality (Theorem 1.1.1), the Archimedean Property (Theorem 1.1.4), and density of the rationals (Theorem 1.1.6). It emphasizes completeness as the distinguishing feature separating rigorous from nonrigorous calculus and devotes significant effort to its consequences, including upper/lower integrals, Lebesgue's existence criterion, limit inferior/superior, and Jordan content zero.
tldr: This is the front matter and opening chapter of an open-access textbook 'Introduction to Real Analysis' by William F. Trench (2013), designed as a rigorous two-term course text for junior/senior mathematics and science majors.
